claims.text: The starting material is equiatomic CoCrFeNi.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNi typically has a single-phase FCC microstructure.
Introducing a few volume percent of a lubricant-forming precursor will produce finely dispersed secondary-phase nanoprecipitates during processing or sliding.
The nanoprecipitates will be uniformly distributed in the CoCrFeNi matrix.
Mechanical and thermal effects during sliding will transform the nanoprecipitates into a continuous or semi-continuous lubricious tribolayer.
The resulting tribolayer will remain thermally stable from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C.
The secondary phase will evolve at the sliding interface into a lubricious stable oxide or layered structure.
The lubricious tribolayer will reduce interfacial shear stress.
The lubricious tribolayer will reduce direct metal-to-metal contact.
Compared with unmodified CoCrFeNi, the modified alloy will have a lower coefficient of friction throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
Compared with unmodified CoCrFeNi, the modified alloy will have a lower wear rate throughout the range from room temperature to 800 °C.
The friction coefficient of unmodified CoCrFeNi increases at elevated temperature.
The wear rate of unmodified CoCrFeNi increases at elevated temperature.
The intervention will be beneficial under moderate-load sliding in air.
Highly corrosive or vacuum environments may compromise formation or stability of the tribolayer.
Load regimes substantially different from moderate loads may compromise formation or stability of the tribolayer.
The intervention's effectiveness depends on nanoprecipitation kinetics and tribolayer-evolution kinetics during sliding.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction exceeding 10% in both average coefficient of friction and wear rate across the tested temperature range, or failure to form the tribolayer consistently, will falsify the hypothesis.
